asking Governor Tina Kotek to get
specific. What more does she want
Portland Public Schools to do? The
governor's calling for more transparency
as the district weighs closing up to 14
schools. Here's a look at the schools
that could be affected. Most are
elementary schools. Tonight, PPS says
it's already held 50 community sessions.
We're also asking Kotek's gubernatorial
challenger, State Senator Christine
Drazan, what more she thinks the
district should do. Thanks for staying
with us at 5. I'm
>> I'm Deborah Knapp. K2 Sunnivie Drazan
joins us live from the PPS headquarters,
which is in North Portland. So,
Sunnivie, who did the governor address
her letter to and what is the district
now saying?
>> So, Deb, the letter was addressed to the
superintendent of Portland Public
Schools and to the board chair, Eddie
Wang. I reached out to the district and
they did give us a response. I called
the chair, Wang, and I did not get a
response back.
On Tuesday, Governor Tina Kotek urged
Portland Public Schools to slow down its
right-sizing process. In a letter, she
wrote, "Since the options for potential
closures were released by your district,
my office has heard from parents,
students, and neighbors expressing shock
and disappointment about the possibility
of losing a neighborhood school and
confusion about the decision-making
timeline and why schools were identified
for change or closure."
She added, "Confusion about the process
is not something we should accept." And
said the district must take time for
families to understand and weigh in
before decisions are made. PPS says it
has been working to keep the community
informed. A district spokesperson wrote
in a statement in part, "We recognize
the deep concerns of our school
communities and are committed to hearing
their voices. Community engagement has
been central to the right-sizing process
from the start and we've already held 50
sessions across the district." We asked
Kotek's office what specific steps it
wants PPS to take before making a
decision. We also asked, "Are you asking
the board to change its timeline? And do
you believe PPS has not done enough due
diligence, or is your concern mainly
whether families understand and can
weigh in on the options?" Her team did
not answer those questions, instead
referring us back to the letter.
>> And if you're a member of the Portland
Public Schools community, your
opportunity to chime in is not over yet.
You can go to our website at katu.com to
see when the next community engagement
sessions are. Reporting live in North
Portland, Tanvi Verma, K2 News.
>> Tanvi, thank you. Well, State Senator
and gubernatorial candidate Christine
Drazan says her office has also heard
from people concerned about proposed
school closures in Portland.
>> Today she called on district leaders to
slow down, listen to families, and be
transparent about how it's making these
decisions. Tanvi also pressed Senator
Drazan on what specifically she wants
the district to do that they're not
already doing.
>> The district has said they've had about
50 community engagement sessions, so
they're a little confused about what the
confusion is. Have you spoken to the
district? Do you see that side?
>> So, I think that there's a difference
between having a community engagement
session and providing the kind of data
and information that would help inform
those sessions.
So, simply saying we're considering
these closures
>> Drazan says the school closures are
driven by enrollment challenges, which
she says can be fixed by improving
student outcomes in schools. She says
she would emphasize that as governor.
The idea to shutter Portland schools is
not new. Last week's announcement on
proposed closures was part of a lengthy
process that started last fall. Tonight,
PPS is more than halfway through that
process. Right now, it's the study and
recommend phase. That means continuing
engagement, collecting feedback, and
finalizing a recommendation. Next is the
decide and commit phase. The
superintendent will present a final
recommendation for the school board to
vote on later this fall. Finally, the
implement phase next school year. And
again, as part of the process, the
district has been hosting engagement
opportunities with the public for
months, more than 50 district-wide so
far. Here are just a few of the upcoming
opportunities over the next week with
more on the calendar next month.
>> As for why the district needs to
right-size, PPS says the move is
necessary to make the district more
stable and sustainable for the future of
all the students. So, the reality is
some elementary middle schools have
fewer students now, and there are a few
reasons for that, including dropping
birth rates, families leaving Portland,
and people simply choosing other
schools. The district argues combining
schools could mean more programs for
students, not less. Under-enrolled
schools cannot offer as many programs
like art and PE. Consolidating schools
would allow for more full-time teachers
and for more balanced class sizes,
according to PPS.
Now, on the flip side, six of the
proposed closures are Title 1 schools,
which serve low-income families. Those
schools get extra federal funding.
>> The district has said it will work with
families to plan transitions and review
whether some communities face greater
impacts. K2's Victor Park went in-depth
on this story last week. You can find
his reporting
on katu.com.

Schools is also considering closing six
elementary schools starting next year,
